sentences.text: The genus name Batrachognathus means "frog jaw" and refers to the animal's short, wide head. The skull is high, short, and broad, measuring 48 mm in length. It possessed 22 or 24 recurved conical teeth in its upper jaws, forming a short and very wide mouth.
Batrachognathus had an orbitoantorbital fenestra, a single opening combining the orbit and antorbital fenestra, similar to that found in monofenestratan pterosaurs.

This small pterosaur had an estimated wingspan of 50 to 75 cm and a body mass of 40 grams, though specimens may not have been adults. The wingspan is estimated at about 50 cm, though David Unwin estimated it to be as large as 75 cm in 2000.
Batrachognathus was a tiny creature with a body mass of only 40 grams.
While the holotype lacks a tail, an undescribed specimen shows that Batrachognathus had a comparatively long tail similar to the related genus Sinomacrops.
The genus Batrachognathus was named in 1948 by the Russian paleontologist Anatoly Nicolaevich Ryabinin.
Three fossils of Batrachognathus have been found in lacustrine sediment in the North-West Tien Shan foothills of the Karatau Mountains.
It is debated whether Batrachognathus had a tail since it was not preserved in the holotype, but it is generally assumed to have had a short tail like other anurognathids.
Batrachognathus was assigned to the family Anurognathidae as a relative of Anurognathus.
In 2003, Alexander Kellner grouped Batrachognathus with the Asian anurognathids Dendrorhynchoides and Jeholopterus into the clade Asiaticognathidae.
A 2021 phylogenetic analysis placed Batrachognathus within the subfamily Batrachognathinae as the sister taxon to the genus Sinomacrops.
Batrachognathus lived during the Late Jurassic (Oxfordian to Kimmeridgian stages) in the Karabastau Formation of Kazakhstan.
Batrachognathus volans lived approximately 150 million years ago during the Oxfordian to Kimmeridgian stages in the Karabastau Svita region of Kazakhstan.
Batrachognathus lived between 161.5 and 154.8 million years ago during the Oxfordian stage.
